extracted.intended_audience: business leaders, CEOs, corporate communications and board members
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on executive speeches and corporate communications focusing on avoiding reputational damage and improving customer-focused strategy and governance. Uses the Ratner case to illustrate lessons for CEOs, communicators and boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the customer
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of economic challenge, a focus on the customer and giving them what they want is paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that even amid recession businesses must 'give consumers what they want' through product, price and service decisions. Example: Ratners' range of fascias targeted distinct price points (Ratners, H Samuel, Watches of Switzerland) which helped dodge the downturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insulting customers in public messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make jokes or remarks that demean your customers; language that mocks customers can destroy reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratner's comments ('Because it’s total crap.'; 'the sandwich will probably last longer than the earrings.') illustrate how joking at customers' expense can provoke a media pile-on and severe commercial consequences. Even if the underlying strategy is sound, 'wrong language' can undo it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose language carefully because words can resurface
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives must be mindful that offhand remarks can resurface later (especially as attitudes change and via social media) and cause reputational damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mike Jeffries' 2006 comments resurfaced in 2013 and led to boycott and retirement; Mike Coupe's filmed behaviour shows how words/acts can haunt leaders. Anticipate long-term reputational risk when speaking publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure independent challenge through board composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards should include non-executive directors and encourage a culture of challenge so leaders receive independent counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues Ratner lacked effective challenge around him; calls for non-execs were a market response. Poor governance and lack of independent oversight contributed to broader corporate failures (e.g., banks 2008, Carillion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test speeches and messages with candid advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: Show speeches and communications to people who will offer honest, challenging feedback rather than seek to please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratner had a director read the speech who merely said it was 'boring' and advised adding a joke — an example of the wrong kind of feedback. Advisers should offer critical challenge, not flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media training and staying 'on message' matter but are not the only lesson
rubrics_metrics.description: While media training and message discipline are important, the deeper issue is governance and the surrounding challenge environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes these are 'not the obvious ones' but acknowledges they remain relevant. The key criticism is that even a message with merit can be undermined by delivery and lack of oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovate and adapt product/promotion strategy during downturns
rubrics_metrics.description: To beat a recession, businesses should innovate, throw out old rules, offer new products, ideas and promotions, and collaborate to lower costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratner urged training staff, communicating with them, incentivising them, and collaborating with the supply chain. Practical tactics: new promotions and product ideas to make life more affordable in a cost-of-living crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage margins but prioritise affordability when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, manage margins — but when consumer spending is squeezed, make life more affordable for customers to sustain demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a balancing criterion: maintain commercial discipline while introducing affordable options and promotions during economic stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your market better than competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: No business can know everything, but winners will know more about their market than their competitors; superior market knowledge underpins success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a strategic imperative rather than a communications tip — gather market intelligence and customer insight to guide product and pricing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the shareholder and market risk of public gaffes
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive gaffes can trigger media frenzy and investor sell-offs that massively destroy shareholder value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratners' share price cratered wiping out £500m of value; this shows how words can translate into immediate financial consequences and the need to weigh communicative risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in communicating around strategic decisions (e.g., acquisitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing expansion or acquisitions, anticipate market and analyst reaction and ensure governance and messaging are robust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratner's remarks about Sterling Jewelers and Kay Jewelers coincided with poor market reaction; leaders should prepare clear, defensible narratives and consult independent advisers before public commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overconfidence and hubris in leadership communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Hubris — believing one is 'too clever' to take counsel — is a risk factor for poor decisions and communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article attributes Ratner's failure partly to arrogance and reluctance to hire capable professionals to provide independent counsel; leaders should guard against overconfidence and welcome scrutiny.
